answer.one_line: Sometimes: fly wiring beat scrambled wiring in 35 of 87 studies, mostly reflex, sensory and steering circuits; in trained, reservoir, ML and our walking tests it tied or lost (34).
answer.short: Of 97 control studies in our catalogue, 87 compare the real wiring with a scrambled or rewired copy: the real wiring helps in 35, makes no difference in 25, does worse in 9, gives mixed results in 15 and is not yet scored in 3. The clear wins are untrained reflex, sensory and steering circuits, while networks trained for machine-learning or game tasks usually do as well with scrambled wiring (a chess-learning mushroom body: 1680 vs 1675 Elo), and a brainless autopilot or a simple rule often matches the fly (Doom 53.3 s vs 51.9 s). The verdict depends on the null: in our own pre-registered test of the sugar reflex, degree-preserving and weight shuffles silence it (0 Hz vs 85 Hz), keeping the sensory and motor boundary keeps about 46% of it, and a sign shuffle makes the whole brain fire. In our own walking test (a FlyGym body driven by the FlyWire brain model through our hand-made mapping), scrambled wiring and a brainless constant drive walked as far as the real brain (14.1 and 14.3 vs 13.9 mm). In our looming test (5-8 Oct 2026), a shadow on one eye turned the fly away in 6 of 6 real-brain body runs and 0 of 3 scrambled body runs (3 more scrambled drives are identical to the no-brain floor, so their walk follows by determinism); scrambled maps silence the steering neurons, scrambled maps turned up to the real map's activity still gave no turn command (3 of 3), and scrambling only the inside of the map kept about -9% of the turn command (none on the far side in all 6 runs) and 69% of the escape signal. The turn command appeared from about 30 per second (38% of our strongest input) on both sides; below that the model did not turn. A steering study on an aircraft rudder (flight-test-the-fly) also finds the wiring helps, yet a classical yaw damper does far better. Most studies are small, single-author and not replicated.

null_types.label: Weight shuffle
null_types.keeps: the graph (who connects to whom), degrees, the weight distribution; usually signs
null_types.destroys: which synapse strength sits on which edge
null_types.question_answered: Does the pattern of synapse strengths matter, given the wiring diagram?
null_types.pitfall: Keeps topology, so it tests weights, not wiring; papers often do not say whether topology is kept.

null_types.label: Degree-preserving rewiring
null_types.keeps: every neuron's in- and out-degree (and often its weights and signs)
null_types.destroys: which specific partners each neuron has
null_types.question_answered: Does the specific partner choice matter beyond each neuron's number of connections?
null_types.pitfall: Rewires the sensory and motor interface too, which can open shortcuts from inputs to outputs (flyconnectome-nulls: 10.7% vs 0.01%); one realisation is not enough.

null_types.label: Random graph (Erdos-Renyi)
null_types.destroys: degree distribution, motifs, modules, partner identity
null_types.question_answered: Does the fly graph beat any random graph of the same size and density?
null_types.pitfall: Easy to beat: also destroys hubs and degree structure, so a win overstates how specific the wiring is.

null_types.label: Target permutation
null_types.keeps: each source neuron's out-degree, weights and signs
null_types.destroys: in-degrees and which targets each neuron reaches
null_types.question_answered: Does it matter where each neuron's outputs go?
null_types.pitfall: In-degrees change, so some neurons get far more or less input; activity levels shift, not just routing.

null_types.label: Sign shuffle
null_types.destroys: which synapses are excitatory and which inhibitory (Dale's law per neuron)
null_types.pitfall: Changes the E/I balance and activity level; a loss may be due to runaway or silent activity, not lost computation.

null_types.label: Boundary-preserving (interior-only) null
null_types.keeps: all sensory-input and descending/motor-output edges; degrees of interior neurons
null_types.question_answered: Does the central wiring matter once the input/output interface is held fixed?
null_types.pitfall: Fairest test of central wiring but weaker: in flyconnectome-nulls it erased the nulls' advantage; interior definition must be declared in advance.

null_types.label: No edges / zero weights
null_types.keeps: the neurons, their models and the input/readout
null_types.question_answered: How much of the result comes from the network at all?
null_types.pitfall: A floor, not a wiring control: almost any network beats it.

null_types.label: Lesion / knockout
null_types.destroys: named neurons or cell types (silenced or removed)
null_types.question_answered: Is this particular neuron or pathway needed?
null_types.pitfall: A null result can mean the controller bypasses the neuron (cyber-larva MDNa: 0.0% change), not that the neuron is unimportant.

null_types.label: No-graph model (MLP, CNN, unconstrained RNN)
null_types.keeps: the task, inputs, outputs and training budget
null_types.question_answered: Does the fly wiring beat a generic learned model?
null_types.pitfall: Parameter counts and tuning effort rarely match; a bigger generic model winning says little about wiring.

null_types.label: Untrained / random parameters
null_types.question_answered: Is the result due to the wiring alone or to training on top of it?
null_types.pitfall: Tests training, not wiring; a connectome-constrained model with random parameters can still show some features (flyvis contrast preference).

null_types.label: Replay (open-loop playback)
null_types.keeps: the recorded input or activity sequence
null_types.destroys: closed-loop coupling between brain and body/world
null_types.question_answered: Does behaviour depend on live feedback through the network?
null_types.pitfall: Replayed activity can look like a working controller; must be compared against live runs on the same scenes.

null_types.label: No-brain baseline (scripted, PD, random policy)
null_types.question_answered: Does the fly network beat a simple controller without a brain?
null_types.pitfall: Baselines often share scaffolding (pilots, CPGs, steering rules) with the brain run, so both may be carried by the same code.

null_types.label: Stimulus absent
null_types.question_answered: Is the behaviour driven by the stimulus rather than by spontaneous or built-in activity?
null_types.pitfall: Shows input dependence, not that the fly wiring is needed; any network can pass it.

null_types.label: Label / target shuffle
null_types.destroys: the pairing of inputs with labels, targets or directions
null_types.pitfall: Only a chance level; says nothing about wiring.

null_types.label: Real fly data
null_types.question_answered: Does the model match animal behaviour or physiology?
null_types.pitfall: A reference, not a null; literature summary statistics may also be the fitting target (not held out).

null_types.label: Other / unclassified
null_types.question_answered: Study-specific (e.g. all-excitatory, binarised weights, input-specificity sets, unverified shuffles)
null_types.pitfall: Must be described in the arm label; not counted as a wiring null.

effect.stat_note: Author statistics: median of per-seed connectome-minus-null differences with 95% CI and Holm p over 4 controls (10 seeds per ecology). Headline difference is the reported median paired difference (-0.199), not 1.57-1.77. Standard nulls beat the connectome; boundary-preserving nulls do not differ (+0.002, -0.074, n.s.).

fairness.reason: All arms evolved with the same budget and 10 seeds, a new null realisation per seed (evo_fix.py:631). Headline N2 keeps degree but not the IO boundary; the boundary-preserving N4/N5 remove the null advantage (standard nulls open sensory-to-descending shortcuts: 10.7% vs 0.01%).
